children: shares fell 8% on Thursday after a report by short-seller Hunterbrook Media raised concerns that the chip company's ties with Chinese entities, some with links to blacklisted firms, could attract greater US regulatory scrutiny.

The report alleges that newer versions of AMD's firmware, essential for its chips to operate in servers, have been incorporated by IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US Department of Commerce in March 2025.

Three companies closely tied to IEIT use the same AMD firmware, the report said, adding that Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California openly sell servers built on AMD chips under their own brands.

AMD also has other ties to blacklisted companies, according to Hunterbrook. "It reported $67 million of licensing income in 2025 that Hunterbrook traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019."
Reuters could not independently verify the report and AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report also raises questions about whether AMD can capitalize on challenges facing rival Nvidia
in China, where US export restrictions have curbed sales of advanced AI chips, most recently through additional tightening announced this week.

Nvidia is facing growing scrutiny over its China business after the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence suspects of spying for China.
AMD appears no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia, despite the recent surge of positive coverage, the Hunterbrook report said.

AMD has a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of 31.28, compared with Intel's 31.55 and Nvidia's 9.83, according to LSEG data. Average rating of 56 analysts covering AMD is "buy" with a median price target of $649.
